title: How AI Reshapes Human Content Creation: The Case of Wikipedia
abstract: We study how Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, affects Wikipedia readership and editing. We compare covered biographies with uncovered biographies in the same field, matched on pre-launch activity and historical characteristics. Over the eight weeks after launch, difference-in-differences estimates imply increases in views and total edits equivalent to 16.2 and 46.5 percent of their pre-launch totals. Lower initial textual similarity predicts larger total-edit responses. Initially more dissimilar pages show more positive subsequent changes in similarity to Grokipedia’s fixed launch-day text, especially where editing is greater. Contributors new to a page account for most of the participation increase, while highly experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share across experience groups. These findings support an inspiration channel: differences in AI-generated content can prompt contributors to revisit and revise Wikipedia entries. AI can therefore stimulate human knowledge production through content supplied on a competing platform.

Email: leungtc@wfu.edu ‡Email: strumpks@wfu.edu 1 1 Introduction Generative AI increasingly produces content that competes with human knowledge on separate platforms. Does this competition crowd out human contribution or prompt additional effort? We study this question through Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia launched as a rival to Wikipedia on October 27, 2025.1 The AI-generated content appears on Grokipedia, while we measure readership, editing and textual changes on Wikipedia. Grokipedia thus provides an external source of competing information, rather than an AI assistant embedded in editors’ work. Because language models draw training material from online content (Dodge et al., 2021), their effects on continued human contribution also matter for the knowledge resources on which future systems can draw. Grokipedia may affect Wikipedia in opposing ways. Readers may turn to the rival, while publicity around its launch may increase interest in topics covered on both platforms. Differences in information or framing may also give Wikipedia editors ideas for additions or revisions. For example, Grokipedia’s launch-day entry discussed anti-communism in Donald Trump’s background, and on October 30 a Wikipedia editor added the category “American Anti-Communists” to his page.2 The timing is suggestive, although we cannot observe whether the editor consulted Grokipedia. Editors may instead deliberately differentiate Wikipedia from its rival. In either case, editors must assess outside information against Wikipedia’s sourcing and neutrality standards, and changes can be contested in discussion or reversed through review. Within these shared rules, individual volunteers decide whether and how to respond to Grokipedia. The net effects on readership, editing and content are therefore ambiguous ex ante and remain an empirical question. We compare Wikipedia biographies covered by Grokipedia with uncovered biographies matched within five fields: Academia, Culture, Leaders, Politics and Sports. The underlying dataset contains approximately 1.4 million pages. Matching uses pre-launch activity 1Although Grokipedia’s sustained visibility was limited, SimilarWeb estimates record about two million worldwide visits on October 28. The economically meaningful changes in Wikipedia activity documented below provide a revealed-preference argument for its relevance. Editors also explicitly discussed Grokipedia as a source of ideas on the archived Talk pages for Turkey (December 8–10, 2025) and RuneScape (November 13, 2025). Recent weekly activity and trends satisfy common mean-balance benchmarks, and the pre-launch weekly comparisons show no systematic pre-trend. We estimate differences in differences using eight weeks before launch, September 1–October 26, and eight weeks afterward, October 27–December 21, 2025. Weekly comparisons trace the response. Wikipedia activity increases relative to matched controls. Over the eight weeks after launch, the preferred estimates imply about 513 additional views and 0.296 additional total edits per page, equivalent to 16.2 and 46.5 percent of the treated pages’ respective pre-launch totals. The estimated increases in views, total edits and minor edits are positive and statistically significant in all five fields. These findings are consistent with an AI-generated rival attracting additional attention and encouraging contributions to Wikipedia. We next ask whether differences between the entries help explain the editing response. Lower initial textual similarity leads to larger total-edit responses, with a smaller effect for minor edits. We then compare weekly Wikipedia versions with each Grokipedia entry’s fixed launch-day text. Pages with larger initial gaps show more positive subsequent changes in similarity, and this relationship is stronger on pages with more editing. The direction of textual change helps distinguish inspiration from deliberate differentiation, since either could generate more revisions where content initially differs. These patterns support an inspiration channel in which differences between entries prompt contributors to revisit a topic and revise its coverage. Revision histories identify who contributes to the increase in participation relative to matched controls. Most comes from contributors new to a page in the observed revision history, and highly experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share across experience groups. Highly experienced editors making their first observed contribution to a page account for 38.7 percent of the total increase. The response therefore draws substantially on experienced Wikipedians becoming active on additional pages. The setting connects two strands of work on generative AI. Studies of direct workplace assistance examine AI used within workers’ production processes, including customer support (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, 2025). Studies of online knowledge communities 3 instead examine participation after ChatGPT becomes available. Burtch, Lee, and Chen (2024) study Stack Overflow and Reddit developer communities, finding declines on Stack Overflow but no evidence of declines on Reddit. del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva, and Wachs (2024) compare Stack Overflow with other question-and-answer communities. Lyu et al. (2025) examine Wikipedia and show that post-ChatGPT changes vary with content overlap. In our setting, Grokipedia supplies an observable rival encyclopedia entry for the same individual, allowing us to connect initial textual distance, human participation, subsequent movement toward a fixed AI-generated text and contributor experience in one cross-platform setting. The results suggest a source of complementarity beyond direct assistance: competing AI-generated content can draw attention to differences between entries and prompt experienced contributors to investigate them. The combination of editing, textual adjustment and editor composition is consistent with this interpretation. Wikipedia’s sourcing and review procedures govern how information encountered elsewhere becomes accepted content. Grokipedia differs from Wikipedia in several ways. In addition to being an AI-based information source, it is an alternative platform that competes for readers and a source based on alternative and unverified sources. And while we frame Wikipedia as a stock of information accumulated by individual editors, another view is that it is an institution that has a centralized response to Grokipedia. We offer evidence that these alternative channels and framings are not too important here. If platform competition was the key mechanism, we would expect strategic differentiation of entries whereas we show there is convergence (as would happen under our view that Wikipedia editors use Grokipedia mainly as an inspiration). Our focus on AI effects is also consistent with other papers in the literature which focus on AI’s impact on information creation on other platforms (Reddit, Stackoverflow, Pixiv). In terms of using alternative sources, our main results continue to hold when we flag references which are blacklisted on Wikipedia. Finally, we might think of Wikipedia as an institution/organization that is coordinating its response to Grokipedia. But Wikipedia is not a traditional institution: it is highly decentralized with editors acting autonomously 4 without any managerial guidance (and they work for free). First, we contribute to the literature on how generative AI shapes user content creation. Empirical studies find that the availability of tools such as ChatGPT is associated with declines in human-authored posts and participation in online communities (Lyu et al., 2025; Burtch, Lee, and Chen, 2024; Glickman and Zhang, 2024; del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva, and Wachs, 2024).3 AI can also complement decentralized knowledge production directly. Evidence from neural machine translation across more than 100 Wikipedia language communities shows increased content creation without reduced quality or readership, with larger gains in better-resourced communities (Zhu and Walker, 2026). Evidence from Pixiv further shows that illustrators exposed to text-to-image AI competition reduce uploads, avoid tags favored by AI-generated content and broaden the intellectual properties they cover (Kim, Jin, and Lee, 2026). Differentiation across artworks is itself valuable on an art platform. Wikipedia and Grokipedia instead seek to document the same underlying subjects and facts, so movement toward the rival text can reflect information transmission. Our setting examines how contributors respond to AI content supplied on a competing platform. We study a different channel: an AI-generated rival on a separate platform, whose content can redirect attention and reveal informational differences without providing Wikipedia contributors with a production tool. Prior expertise may matter differently when AI supplies an external source to evaluate than when it directly assists a task. In customer support, AI assistance produces especially large productivity gains among novice and lower-skilled workers (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, 2025). A three-month patent-lawyer experiment similarly finds larger assisted-drafting gains among juniors, but subsequent gains on an unaided judgment task are concentrated among seniors (Autor et al., 2026). These results suggest that expertise can shape how people respond to AI-generated information. We contribute to this ongoing literature in another environment: volunteer participation in response to a rival encyclopedia. Experienced editors may face lower costs of checking unfamiliar claims and reconciling them with Wikipedia’s sourcing and neutrality standards. An alternative encyclopedia entry could consequently draw their attention to pages where that expertise is useful. 31 7 Conclusion Grokipedia’s launch increased readership and editing on covered Wikipedia pages relative to matched controls. Over the eight weeks after launch, the estimated increases amount to 16.2 percent of pre-launch views and 46.5 percent of pre-launch total edits. Pages with less initial textual overlap have larger total-edit responses, with the similarity gradient concentrated in non-minor edits. Initially more dissimilar Wikipedia pages also move relatively closer to Grokipedia’s fixed launch-day text, particularly where editing is more intensive. This relative convergence weighs against strategic differentiation as the primary response to the rival platform and supports the inspiration channel. Most of the increase in participation comes from contributors new to a page in the observed revision history. Highly experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share across experience groups, indicating that the response draws substantially on established contributors becoming active on additional pages. Future work could examine how these responses develop over longer periods, affect the quality and neutrality of Wikipedia content (Greenstein and Zhu, 2012), and shape public trust in Wikipedia amid AI competition (Hinnosaar et al., 2023). These findings suggest that competing AI-generated content can encourage human contribution by drawing attention to differences in coverage or framing. Contributors decide which pages to edit and how to revise them, while Wikipedia’s sourcing and review procedures govern the resulting content. The Case of Wikipedia ∗

Abstract
We study how Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, affects Wikipedia
readership and editing. We compare covered biographies with uncovered biogra-
phies in the same field, matched on pre-launch activity and historical character-
istics. Over the eight weeks after launch, difference-in-differences estimates imply
increases in views and total edits equivalent to 16.2 and 46.5 percent of their pre-
launch totals. Lower initial textual similarity predicts larger total-edit responses.
Initially more dissimilar pages show more positive subsequent changes in similarity
to Grokipedia’s fixed launch-day text, especially where editing is greater. Contrib-
utors new to a page account for most of the participation increase, while highly
experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share across experience groups.
These findings support an inspiration channel: differences in AI-generated content
can prompt contributors to revisit and revise Wikipedia entries. AI can therefore
stimulate human knowledge production through content supplied on a competing
platform.

1 Introduction
Generative AI increasingly produces content that competes with human knowledge on
separate platforms. Does this competition crowd out human contribution or prompt ad-
ditional effort? We study this question through Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia
launched as a rival to Wikipedia on October 27, 2025.1 The AI-generated content appears
on Grokipedia, while we measure readership, editing and textual changes on Wikipedia.
Grokipedia thus provides an external source of competing information, rather than an
AI assistant embedded in editors’ work. Because language models draw training material
from online content (Dodge et al., 2021), their effects on continued human contribution
also matter for the knowledge resources on which future systems can draw.
Grokipedia may affect Wikipedia in opposing ways. Readers may turn to the rival,
while publicity around its launch may increase interest in topics covered on both platforms.
Differences in information or framing may also give Wikipedia editors ideas for additions
or revisions. For example, Grokipedia’s launch-day entry discussed anti-communism in
Donald Trump’s background, and on October 30 a Wikipedia editor added the category
“American Anti-Communists” to his page.2 The timing is suggestive, although we cannot
observe whether the editor consulted Grokipedia. Editors may instead deliberately differ-
entiate Wikipedia from its rival. In either case, editors must assess outside information
against Wikipedia’s sourcing and neutrality standards, and changes can be contested in
discussion or reversed through review. Within these shared rules, individual volunteers
decide whether and how to respond to Grokipedia. The net effects on readership, editing
and content are therefore ambiguous ex ante and remain an empirical question.
We compare Wikipedia biographies covered by Grokipedia with uncovered biographies
matched within five fields: Academia, Culture, Leaders, Politics and Sports. The under-
lying dataset contains approximately 1.4 million pages. Matching uses pre-launch activity

worldwide visits on October 28. The economically meaningful changes in Wikipedia activity docu-
mented below provide a revealed-preference argument for its relevance. Editors also explicitly discussed
Grokipedia as a source of ideas on the archived Talk pages for Turkey (December 8–10, 2025) and
RuneScape (November 13, 2025). These discussions concern possible improvements, not verified in-

histories and historical characteristics, yielding 80,909 treated pages. Recent weekly ac-
tivity and trends satisfy common mean-balance benchmarks, and the pre-launch weekly
comparisons show no systematic pre-trend. We estimate differences in differences using
eight weeks before launch, September 1–October 26, and eight weeks afterward, October
27–December 21, 2025. Weekly comparisons trace the response.
Wikipedia activity increases relative to matched controls. Over the eight weeks after
launch, the preferred estimates imply about 513 additional views and 0.296 additional
total edits per page, equivalent to 16.2 and 46.5 percent of the treated pages’ respective
pre-launch totals. The estimated increases in views, total edits and minor edits are
positive and statistically significant in all five fields. These findings are consistent with
an AI-generated rival attracting additional attention and encouraging contributions to
Wikipedia.
We next ask whether differences between the entries help explain the editing response.
Lower initial textual similarity leads to larger total-edit responses, with a smaller effect
for minor edits. We then compare weekly Wikipedia versions with each Grokipedia en-
try’s fixed launch-day text. Pages with larger initial gaps show more positive subsequent
changes in similarity, and this relationship is stronger on pages with more editing. The
direction of textual change helps distinguish inspiration from deliberate differentiation,
since either could generate more revisions where content initially differs. These patterns
support an inspiration channel in which differences between entries prompt contributors
to revisit a topic and revise its coverage.
Revision histories identify who contributes to the increase in participation relative to
matched controls. Most comes from contributors new to a page in the observed revision
history, and highly experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share across experi-
ence groups. Highly experienced editors making their first observed contribution to a page
account for 38.7 percent of the total increase. The response therefore draws substantially
on experienced Wikipedians becoming active on additional pages.
The setting connects two strands of work on generative AI. Studies of direct workplace
assistance examine AI used within workers’ production processes, including customer
support (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, 2025). Studies of online knowledge communities
3

instead examine participation after ChatGPT becomes available. Burtch, Lee, and Chen
(2024) study Stack Overflow and Reddit developer communities, finding declines on Stack
Overflow but no evidence of declines on Reddit. del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva, and
Wachs (2024) compare Stack Overflow with other question-and-answer communities. Lyu
et al. (2025) examine Wikipedia and show that post-ChatGPT changes vary with content
overlap. In our setting, Grokipedia supplies an observable rival encyclopedia entry for
the same individual, allowing us to connect initial textual distance, human participation,
subsequent movement toward a fixed AI-generated text and contributor experience in one
cross-platform setting.
The results suggest a source of complementarity beyond direct assistance: compet-
ing AI-generated content can draw attention to differences between entries and prompt
experienced contributors to investigate them. The combination of editing, textual adjust-
ment and editor composition is consistent with this interpretation. Wikipedia’s sourcing
and review procedures govern how information encountered elsewhere becomes accepted
content.
Grokipedia differs from Wikipedia in several ways. In addition to being an AI-based
information source, it is an alternative platform that competes for readers and a source
based on alternative and unverified sources. And while we frame Wikipedia as a stock of
information accumulated by individual editors, another view is that it is an institution
that has a centralized response to Grokipedia.
We offer evidence that these alternative channels and framings are not too impor-
tant here. If platform competition was the key mechanism, we would expect strategic
differentiation of entries whereas we show there is convergence (as would happen under
our view that Wikipedia editors use Grokipedia mainly as an inspiration). Our focus on
AI effects is also consistent with other papers in the literature which focus on AI’s im-
pact on information creation on other platforms (Reddit, Stackoverflow, Pixiv). In terms
of using alternative sources, our main results continue to hold when we flag references
which are blacklisted on Wikipedia. Finally, we might think of Wikipedia as an insti-
tution/organization that is coordinating its response to Grokipedia. But Wikipedia is
not a traditional institution: it is highly decentralized with editors acting autonomously
4

without any managerial guidance (and they work for free).
Section 2 reviews related work, and Section 3 describes the setting. Sections 4 and 5
present the model and data. Section 6 reports the empirical design and results, followed
by the conclusion.
2 Literature
Our study contributes to research on generative AI, platform competition and voluntary
knowledge production.
First, we contribute to the literature on how generative AI shapes user content cre-
ation. Empirical studies find that the availability of tools such as ChatGPT is associated
with declines in human-authored posts and participation in online communities (Lyu et al.,
2025; Burtch, Lee, and Chen, 2024; Glickman and Zhang, 2024; del Rio-Chanona, Lau-
rentsyeva, and Wachs, 2024).3 AI can also complement decentralized knowledge produc-
tion directly. Evidence from neural machine translation across more than 100 Wikipedia
language communities shows increased content creation without reduced quality or reader-
ship, with larger gains in better-resourced communities (Zhu and Walker, 2026). Evidence
from Pixiv further shows that illustrators exposed to text-to-image AI competition reduce
uploads, avoid tags favored by AI-generated content and broaden the intellectual proper-
ties they cover (Kim, Jin, and Lee, 2026). Differentiation across artworks is itself valuable
on an art platform. Wikipedia and Grokipedia instead seek to document the same un-
derlying subjects and facts, so movement toward the rival text can reflect information
transmission. Our setting examines how contributors respond to AI content supplied on
a competing platform.
We study a different channel: an AI-generated rival on a separate platform, whose
content can redirect attention and reveal informational differences without providing
Wikipedia contributors with a production tool. We find that this competitive entry
3Our results also relate to research on whether generative AI complements or substitutes for human skills
(Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond, 2025; Acemoglu et al., 2022). Wikipedia contributors are unpaid and
their output is freely available, so pro-social motives may shape their responses differently from those of
paid workers. We also study knowledge creation rather than employment outcomes such as productivity
or wages.
5

stimulates, rather than displaces, human contribution. This aligns with recent work on
“human-in-the-loop” systems where AI serves as a “recombinant” tool, lowering the search
costs for identifying knowledge gaps or framing new ideas (Agrawal, Gans, and Goldfarb,
2018). Our results suggest that AI-generated content serves as a reference point that
highlights missing information or alternative perspectives. In other words, AI activates
an “inspiration” channel: its novel framing and distinct informational content make gaps
in the existing record salient, prompting editors to engage in expansionary and integrative
work to close the distance between the platforms. 4
Second, our findings connect to the literature on digital platform competition and
strategic differentiation. Standard models of platform entry suggest that when a low-
cost, automated entrant (Grokipedia) appears, the incumbent platform (Wikipedia) faces
pressure to differentiate (Eisenmann, Parker, and Van Alstyne, 2011; Zhu and Iansiti,
2012). We study the response of Wikipedia’s volunteer editors to this entry.
Our model emphasizes changes in reader attention and editors’ responses to differences
between entries. These channels can change contribution even when editing costs remain
unchanged. This differs from the cost channel in Gans (2024), where AI reduces the
cost of low-complexity tasks and shifts human effort toward harder problems through a
free-rider threshold effect.
Third, we contribute to the literature on the private provision of public goods, particu-
larly in online knowledge commons.5 Prior work establishes that contributors to platforms
like Wikipedia are motivated by peer recognition, social impact, and audience size (Zhang
and Zhu, 2011; Gallus, 2017; Hinnosaar et al., 2022). Related field-experimental evidence
from Zhihu distinguishes contribution-specific recognition from broader status signals:
Zhang and Luo (2026) find that exogenously increasing peer upvotes raises subsequent
answer volume, length, and quality, whereas adding followers has little overall effect. They
interpret this contrast as consistent with peer recognition reinforcing intrinsic motivation,
while follower counts function more as status signals. A key concern in this literature is

ated Wikipedia entry (Triedman and Mantzarlis, 2025; Yasseri, 2025). We examine changes in Wikipedia
readership, editing and text following Grokipedia’s entry.

whether automated content generation will erode these intrinsic motivations by making
human effort feel redundant.
Our findings add a role for competing AI-generated content in voluntary knowledge
production. Editing responses are larger on pages with lower initial textual similarity to
Grokipedia, and highly experienced contributors account for the largest share of the par-
ticipation response across experience groups. External AI content can therefore encourage
established volunteers to become active on additional pages. This finding connects vol-
untary contribution to research on how automation changes the tasks people perform
(Autor, Levy, and Murnane, 2003).
3 Background on Wikipedia and Grokipedia
Wikipedia editors are responsible for verifiability, factual accuracy, reliable sourcing and
neutrality, including when they use AI tools. Official guidelines allow AI-assisted drafting
and editing but require substantive human review (Wikipedia contributors, 2024). The
Wikimedia Foundation’s AI strategy likewise treats generative models as tools to assist
volunteer contributors (Owen, 2025).
Concerns about hallucinated citations, generic prose and unverifiable claims have led
editors to strengthen safeguards against unreviewed AI content (Heater, 2025). In 2025,
Wikipedia introduced a speedy deletion mechanism for articles suspected of being unvet-
ted AI output (Hale, 2025). AI-assisted editing thus requires volunteers to check claims,
repair citations and revise text to meet community standards. The Wikimedia Foundation
also addressed the rise of generative AI encyclopedias in a November 10, 2025 blog post,
emphasizing Wikipedia’s value less than two weeks after Grokipedia’s launch (Wikimedia
Foundation, 2025b).
This policy environment makes Grokipedia a useful setting for studying the entry of an
AI-native encyclopedia positioned as a competitor to Wikipedia, built in conjunction with
xAI’s “Grok” large language model.6 Launched on October 27, 2025, its stated purpose is

We compare each Grokipedia entry at its October 27, 2025 launch version with the corre-

are available. Stable person and page identifiers link biographies across platforms. 14 The

Our hybrid similarity measure combines semantic overlap in meaning with lexical
overlap in wording.
The first component uses the transformer-based embedding model all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
It represents text as a vector and measures semantic overlap by the cosine between the
two vectors. Texts can be close in this representation even when they describe the same
events using different words or sentence structures. For example, two biographies may
describe the same career trajectory while emphasizing different episodes or arranging
them differently. This component is intended to capture overlap in meaning beyond exact
wording.15
The second component uses TF–IDF cosine similarity to measure lexical overlap. The
vectorizer is fitted to each pair of texts and weights words by their frequency and relative
informativeness within that pair. Shared names, dates and terminology raise similarity,
whereas wording changes can lower it even when the underlying facts are the same. This
component is thus more sensitive to close textual reproduction than the semantic repre-
sentation. Conversely, it can treat a paraphrase as less similar even when it conveys much
the same information.
The two components respond to different aspects of encyclopedic content. ForRodney
(wrestler), the recorded TF–IDF score is 0.860 and the embedding score is 0.772. The
texts share biographical material, names and wrestling terminology, while differing in
presentation. The example illustrates why lexical and semantic measures need not agree.
The hybrid score places weight 0.6 on embedding similarity and 0.4 on TF–IDF sim-
ilarity. The greater embedding weight reflects our interest in content overlap, while the
lexical component retains information about close wording. All reported regressions use
this measure.

Prior expertise may matter differently when AI supplies an external source to eval-

especially large productivity gains among novice and lower-skilled workers (Brynjolfsson,

Experienced editors may face lower costs of checking unfamiliar claims and reconciling
them with Wikipedia’s sourcing and neutrality standards. An alternative encyclopedia
entry could consequently draw their attention to pages where that expertise is useful.

7 Conclusion
Grokipedia’s launch increased readership and editing on covered Wikipedia pages relative
to matched controls. Over the eight weeks after launch, the estimated increases amount
to 16.2 percent of pre-launch views and 46.5 percent of pre-launch total edits. Pages with
less initial textual overlap have larger total-edit responses, with the similarity gradient
concentrated in non-minor edits. Initially more dissimilar Wikipedia pages also move
relatively closer to Grokipedia’s fixed launch-day text, particularly where editing is more
intensive. This relative convergence weighs against strategic differentiation as the primary
response to the rival platform and supports the inspiration channel.
Most of the increase in participation comes from contributors new to a page in the
observed revision history. Highly experienced Wikipedians account for the largest share
across experience groups, indicating that the response draws substantially on established
contributors becoming active on additional pages.
Future work could examine how these responses develop over longer periods, affect
the quality and neutrality of Wikipedia content (Greenstein and Zhu, 2012), and shape
public trust in Wikipedia amid AI competition (Hinnosaar et al., 2023).
These findings suggest that competing AI-generated content can encourage human
contribution by drawing attention to differences in coverage or framing. Contributors
decide which pages to edit and how to revise them, while Wikipedia’s sourcing and review
procedures govern the resulting content. AI can therefore stimulate voluntary knowledge
production through content supplied on a competing platform.

title: Measuring Media Bias Through Homepage Duration: Evidence from NYT and WSJ
abstract: We introduce a duration-based measure of newsroom emphasis based on the time articles remain on digital homepages. Using data on more than 100,000 NYT and WSJ articles and 24 million tweets, we examine how reader-engagement proxies and article slant jointly predict homepage survival. For the NYT, more pro-Democrat articles remain longer after conditioning on demand controls. For the WSJ, analogous slant associations are weaker overall and concentrated in selected subsets. The patterns are consistent with editorial weighting that is diﬀicult to reconcile with a purely demand-based interpretation, but they are not definitive causal evidence of supply-side bias. Profit-maximizing outlets may also give greater prominence to content that best retains their core audiences. The results therefore provide a duration-based measurement approach and disciplined descriptive facts for future work on mechanisms.

title: Digital Social Pressure, Managerial Decision-Making and Worker Performance: Evidence from Professional Football
abstract: Digital platforms expose workers and managers to immediate, public, and persistent evaluations from external audiences, creating a form of social pressure that may shape workplace decisions. We examine whether such digital social pressure predicts subsequent opportunity allocation and worker performance, using professional football as a high-frequency empirical setting. We link player-match data from Europe’s five major leagues to post-match Twitter commentary and construct measures of negative sentiment, toxicity, and racial abuse. Comparing players with themselves over time and teammates in the same current match, we find that greater negative sentiment is associated with a lower probability of appearing in the team’s next match. Toxicity shows a similar but less stable association, while racial-abuse intensity is imprecisely estimated when the measures enter jointly. By contrast, associations with performance conditional on a subsequent appearance are small and imprecise. Overall, the findings suggest that digital social pressure is reflected more strongly in the allocation of subsequent opportunities than in worker performance, showing how public evaluations generated outside formal organizational boundaries can become part of the reputational environment surrounding internal managerial decisions.

title: Dissecting Netflix's Self-Preferencing: Evidence from Viewer-Level Data
abstract: This paper studies self-preferencing in subscription video streaming. We assemble a new dataset linking Netflix’s U.S. catalog, Top 10 rankings, Wikipedia page views, and device-level streaming records. Conditional on external popularity and other observables, Netflix Originals are significantly more likely to appear in the Top 10 than comparable non-original titles, especially among series. Using a matched staggered difference-in-differences design around first Top 10 entry, we show that Top 10 placement causally increases subsequent viewership. The effect is weaker among devices with extensive prior Netflix viewing, consistent with personalized recommendations substituting for generic rankings. These findings provide evidence of platform gatekeeping in digital media.

title: Experimentation Without Exit: Multihoming and Platform Persistence in #EconTwitter
abstract: We study the attempted migration of the #EconTwitter community from Twitter/X to Mastodon following Elon Musk’s acquisition of the platform. Leveraging a dataset of 4.3 million tweets from over 2,000 economists—including detailed records of their weekly activity and network-mediated exposure to peers’ Mastodon-related retweets—we examine how peer discussions relate to platform engagement. In a difference-in-differences framework, we estimate that greater exposure to Mastodon-related discussions is followed by a short-run decline in activity on Twitter/X. However, this relationship attenuates substantially when we control for economist fixed effects or examine longer-run behavior. Two years later, economists with higher Mastodon exposure are somewhat more likely to multi-home across platforms but only marginally less active on Twitter/X. These findings highlight the strength of network effects and the difficulty of disrupting incumbent platforms, even during periods of widespread discontent.

title: An Empirical Decomposition of Information vs Sentiment Shifts in Advertising
abstract: Advertising influences market expectations through three distinct pathways: raising awareness, shaping sentiment, and providing information. This paper empirically disentangles these effects using movie trailers as an empirical setting, leveraging a dataset of nearly 600 wide-release U.S. films (2017-2021). We analyze how trailer releases affect pre-theatrical demand expectations, as reflected in Hollywood Stock Exchange (HSX) prices, and measure the three channels of consumer engagement through Twitter discussions and Wikipedia page views. Our findings show that trailers significantly boost HSX prices, particularly for non-sequels with lower prior awareness. While heightened engagement correlates with stronger market expectations, additional informational content can sometimes dampen enthusiasm. Moreover, trailer releases reduces uncertainty, as evidenced by a decline in HSX price volatility for non-sequels. By disentangling the three pathways of advertising influence, this study contributes to the literature on advertising effectiveness and offers actionable insights for marketers optimizing promotional strategies in a digital landscape.

title: Quantifying Racial Prejudices with Housing Transaction Data
abstract: This paper aims to quantify racial prejudices using transaction-level housing market data. We pin down the impact of a marginal change of racial composition in a narrowly-defined neighborhood on the price appreciation between repeated sales of a house, and we find that an additional nonwhite household within a radius of 0.2 miles reduces the price appreciation by 1.27 percentage points. The effects are weaker in neighborhoods with a thicker housing market and a higher income level, suggesting that the role of racial prejudices is limited by market forces. The effects are also associated with voting behaviors and public anti-racism statements made on social media, indicating that they are likely to be driven by taste-based racial preferences. While we also find evidence of racial price discrimination effects as in the literature, these effects tend to be a form of statistical discrimination driven by other factors that correlate with race.

title: All the Headlines that Are Fit to Change
abstract: We study how the New York Times changes headlines after an article has been published. We track the 35,000 articles on the newspaper’s home page between February 2021 and April 2022, and find that 10% have an immediate headline change while another 11% undergo an A/B test where two titles are trialed against one another over a short time window. We also collect every tweet of an article in our data. We first look at which articles get a headline change of some form. Article type matters: popularity on Twitter, hard news, negative sentiment headline, and mentions from more partisan Twitter accounts are associated with headline changes. Another factor is social pressure, negative tweets from users connected to the reporter or the newspaper, which leads to more immediate headline changes and to a lesser extent to A/B tests. Next we examine how headline changes impact an article’s performance metrics. After accounting for selection, we find that headline changes increase an article’s popularity. There is also evidence that headline changes increase the negative sentiment and liberal political slant when it is tweeted. We also analyze headline changes at the Wall Street Journal for a shorter period, and find comparable behavior. Our results have implications for distinguishing supply and demand driven models of media bias, how digitization may foster media consolidation, and conditions under which economic or partisan motives drive newspaper decision-making.

title: Globalization and the Rise of Action Movies in Hollywood,
abstract: This paper shows that Globalization contributes significantly to the rise of Action movies in Hollywood. Incorporating both the intensive and extensive margins in trade, this paper develops a structural model to allow movie-quality production heterogeneity across genres and countries. The paper finds that Hollywood studios respond to export-market expansion by tailoring their products to international consumers’ preferences. As a result, Hollywood increasingly focuses on a few blockbusters, overwhelmingly in the Action genre. The movie industry becomes significantly more concentrated both domestically and abroad. Furthermore, a disproportionate increase in Action movies raises consumer welfare in some countries at other regions’ expense.

title: Eliminating Digital Rights Management in the E-Book Market,
abstract: We examine the impact of removing Digital Rights Management (DRM) from electronic book devices. We derive a Bayesian hierarchical logit model based on the consumer’s utility maximization problem and estimate the model using data from a choice-based survey. We then simulate the counterfactual market outcomes when DRM is removed; on average, the consumer surplus increases nontrivially holding everything else constant. However, the gain in consumer surplus is diminished when we re-calibrate e-book device prices. Further, if there is a negative shock to content supply, then the consumer surplus could in fact decrease after DRM removal.

title: Why Are Inferior Seats "Underpriced"? Evidence from the English Premier League
abstract: This paper studies the practice of loss-leader pricing strategy in the English Premier League (EPL). While the TV broadcasting revenue for EPL clubs has increased over the past 20 years, the importance of revenue from ticket sales has declined. The theory of multi-product pricing suggests that a change in the relative importance of revenue sources can induce profit-maximizing firms to underprice one product in order to raise the demand for a complementary one. Using other leagues in England and Scotland that do not have as much TV broadcasting revenue as a control group, we find that inferior seats are underpriced among the ELP clubs. Consistent with the growing importance of TV broadcast revenue, we also find that such "loss-leader pricing" is stronger in later years of the sample. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the underpricing of inferior seats is more pronounced in (i) EPL clubs compared to clubs in other European leagues; (ii) elite clubs in ELP compared to non-elite clubs in ELP that have less TV broadcasting revenue; and (iii) clubs promoted to ELP as compared to clubs that are either promoted or relegated to different leagues in England and Scotland. These findings suggest that clubs that rely more on TV broadcasting underprice their inferior seats as loss leader to attract more passionate fans.

abstract: Consumers can only choose to see a movie if it is available in theaters. Explicitly taking into account movie theater availability, we estimate a structural model of movie demand with the use of U.S. movie data from 1995 to 2017. Estimation results indicate that the impact of theater availability on movie demand is both statistically and economically significant. We also find that movie budget predictions based on the model that incorporates theater availability is more consistent with the data, while the model that ignores theater availability on average over-predict production budgets.

title: What Can Regulators Deregulate? The Case of Electricity,
abstract: We revisit Stigler and Friedland’s (J Law Econ 5:1–16, 1962) seminal paper by examining how competitive generation affects prices, sustainability, and reliability in the electricity industry. Exploiting state and year variation in the introduction of regional transmission organizations (RTOs) that facilitate open access to transmission, we first show that wholesale market deregulation significantly increases the prevalence of independent power producers (IPPs). Using RTO membership as an instrument, we find that IPP entry fails to cut electricity prices paid by consumers. This non-result is also robust to using initial electricity tariffs as an instrument for changes in IPP in a long-difference specification. We provide suggestive evidence that the absence of consumer gain can be attributed to efficiency loss due to mandated divestiture of generation assets or simply higher upstream transaction costs. But, increased prevalence of IPPs is associated with more solar and hydropower, although the use of non-fossil fuel as a whole remains unchanged because less nuclear power is used. More IPPs, however, is also associated with less reliable electricity supply. A review of the origins of electricity deregulation suggests that this tradeoff between environmental sustainability and energy security is not likely to have been the major determinant of the deregulation. Rather than a pro-consumer deregulation, the regulatory change is perhaps more appropriately interpreted as a regulatory capture that benefits IPP entrants and existing energy marketers.

title: Tax-driven Bunching of Housing Market Transactions: The Case of Hong Kong,
abstract: We study the implications of a property market transaction tax. As property buyers are obligated to pay a transaction tax (“stamp duty” or SD) where the rate increases with the value of the transaction, there are incentives to trade at the cutoff points of the tax schedule or just below them. Thus, both “bunching in transactions” and “underpricing” should be observed near those cutoffs. Furthermore, the bunching points should change with the tax schedule. We confirm these conjectures with a rich dataset from the Hong Kong housing market and provide a measure of tax avoidance.

title: Music Piracy: Bad for Record Sales but Good for the iPod?
abstract: Music piracy is a double-edged sword for the music industry. On the one hand, it hurts record sales. On the other hand, it increases sales of its complements. To quantify the effect of music piracy, I construct a unique survey data set and use a Bayesian method to estimate the demand for music and iPods, and ﬁnd three things. First, music piracy decreases music sales by 24% to 42%. Second, music piracy contributes 12% to iPod sales. Finally, counterfactual experiments show that, if music were free, the increase in Apple’s proﬁts from iPod can more than compensate the loss of musicians. The last result implies that a Pareto improving iPod tax is possible.

title: Love Thy Neighbor: Income Distribution and Housing Preferences,
abstract: Do homeowners prefer living in an area with a more equal distribution of income? We answer this question by estimating a semi-parametric hedonic pricing model for about 90,000 housing units transacted in Hong Kong between 2005 and 2006. We ﬁrst identify a hedonic price function by locally regressing the rental price of the housing unit on its intrinsic and neighborhood characteristics, one of which is the Gini coefﬁcient for household income of the constituency area. We then combine the estimates with a log utility function to obtain the heterogeneous preference parameters. Finally, we estimate the joint distribution of the preference parameters and demographics. We ﬁnd that most homeowners have a strong distaste for inequality in their neighborhood, and the distaste increases with income and goes down with education level. Counterfactual experiments show that reallocating public rental housing by half can increase the welfare of homeowners by about HK$8,000 on average per year, an amount which is equivalent to increasing the housing unit by 20 square feet or reducing the age of the unit by 5 years.

with ourselves’’
Of the Imitation of Christ , Thomas à Kempis
(1418).
Do homeowners have a preference for living among
neighbors with a similar income level? Common sense
suggests that homeowners prefer income equality in the
neighborhood. There is the alleged snobbery of the rich to-
wards the poor and the reciprocal jealousy of the poor to-
wards the rich. Recent neural science research has also
shown that humans have social preferences to reduce
inequality in outcome distributions (see Tricomi et al.,
2010). According to one sociological research by Gans
(1961), ‘‘People with higher incomes and more education
may feel that they or their children are being harmed by
living among less advantaged neighbors. The latter are
likely to feel equally negative about the ‘airs’ being put
on by the former ... ’’. In this paper we give a quantitative
answer
